title: Rate limiter design
idea: A rate limiter decides, per client key, whether a request may run now, and refuses the rest so one caller cannot flood a service.

analogy.text: An arcade coin jar. A tap drips one coin in each second, the jar holds three, and every game costs one coin.
analogy.breaks: Real tokens are only a number, recomputed when a request arrives.

points: Every limiter answers one question: may this key make a request now?
Token bucket: tokens refill at a steady rate, and each request spends one.
Sliding window log: keep recent request times and refuse once the window is full.
Algorithms share one `RateLimiter` interface, so callers swap them without edits.

steps.caption: A new key starts with a full bucket of three tokens. Four requests arrive almost together.
Request 1 spends a token and goes through.
Requests 2 and 3 spend the last two tokens. The burst capacity is used up.
Request 4 finds the bucket empty and is refused at once. It is not queued.
A second passes. The refill adds one token, computed from elapsed time on the next call.
Request 5 spends the fresh token. Long-run rate: one per second, bursts up to three.

code.title: Token bucket
code.caption: Time is passed in as milliseconds, so the run is repeatable. Change the bucket to `new TokenBucket(1, 2)` and predict the output.

walk.text: The interface: one method, `allow(key, nowMs)`, returning `true` or `false`.
One bucket per key, so each client has its own allowance.
No timer runs. Tokens are topped up from elapsed time, capped at capacity.
Below one token, refuse. Otherwise spend one and allow.
Three pass, the fourth fails. A different key has its own full bucket.
One second after the burst, one token has refilled: one passes, the next fails.
After a long idle gap the bucket is full again, but never above three.

code.title: Sliding window log
code.caption: Same `allow(key, nowMs)` method as the `RateLimiter` interface, a different rule: at most two requests in any rolling second.

walk.text: Each key keeps a list of the times it was allowed.
Drop times older than the window. What is left is recent traffic.
Allow only if the window holds fewer than the limit, and record it.
At 1000 the request at 0 has left the window, so there is room again.

pitfalls: Limit per user or API key, not with one global counter for everyone.
A fixed window resets each clock second, so two full bursts can land 1 ms apart.
An in-process `Map` limits one server only; several servers need a shared store.

quiz.why: A fixed window counts per clock second. 999 ms and 1000 ms fall in different windows, so a client can spend a full limit in each.

takeaway: Hide the algorithm behind `allow(key, now)` and keep one allowance per key.

starters: When should I choose token bucket over sliding window?
How would I build this rate limiter on Redis for many servers?
How do I stop the per-key map from growing forever?
